claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is a dense, single-phase BCC alloy.
The baseline alloy has high yield strength.
The baseline alloy has limited room-temperature ductility.
Brittle phase formation and high atomic mass cause the baseline alloy's limited room-temperature ductility.
Replacing part of Hf and Zr with V or Nb reduces the alloy's bulk density.
Adding 0.1-0.5 at% interstitial oxygen promotes nucleation of coherent nanoscale precipitates in the modified alloy.
Light-element substitution, oxygen addition, and thermomechanical processing produce a dual-phase microstructure.
The proposed microstructure consists of a ductile BCC matrix reinforced by coherent nanoscale oxide or carbide precipitates.
The proposed processing route refines the alloy's grain size.
The coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
Grain-boundary strengthening improves ductility in the proposed alloy.
Refined grains and the second phase promote strain hardening and delay necking, thereby improving ductility.
The modified alloy will have a density more than 5% below that of the baseline.
The modified alloy will have a yield strength more than 10% above that of the baseline.
The modified alloy will have an elongation to failure more than 20% above that of the baseline at room temperature.
Oxygen concentrations above 0.5 at% lead to large, brittle oxide networks.
Excessive V or Nb substitution may destabilize the BCC phase and form brittle sigma or Laves phases.
Solution treatment at 1200-1400°C followed by aging at 800-1000°C is an appropriate processing window for the proposed alloy.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as single-phase BCC, yet its limited ductility is simultaneously attributed to brittle phase formation; the nature or location of this additional brittle phase is not reconciled with the single-phase description.
The intervention introduces oxygen but no carbon source, whereas the proposed mediator includes carbide precipitates without specifying how carbides would form.
